utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon, Witness 28. I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony this last Friday. I further would like to remind the parties that if any question is put to the witness which might result in an answer that could reveal her identity, that we should go into private session well in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally, I would like to remind the parties that microphones should be switched off when the witness answers questions. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness 28. Can I just announce we do have a redacted version of the statement in e-court, and I understand it's Exhibit P1211 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologies. We do not hear Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, there seems to be a technical problem. Mr. Re, perhaps the other microphone is better.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I -- can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: On Thursday afternoon, I was asking you some questions, Witness 28, about some portions of your statement. I just want to take you to paragraph 29 of your statement - and I understand you have a copy in front of you - which reads: "A MUP officer in Decani, whose name I can no longer recall, told me that around the same time" -- that was in early March 1998 or so -- "the bridge in Jablanica was destroyed, most likely by the KLA, to prevent the MUP from entering Jablanica and patrolling the area." My question is this - and I appreciate it's been a long time, and to an extent you're relying upon your memory - can you provide the Trial Chamber with any further -- any more details about the bridge or what you were told about its destruction around that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really too much more than I already said. Just circumstances of that discussion I can maybe remember. That was the time when policeman Prascevic was killed. That was the beginning of the March. I travelled to Decani. I talked to his wife. I think related to that murder was also Valeta Hirej [phoen] case and [indiscernible]. And then I visited also the police station in Decani to talk what is happening and what's behind that. And that was that discussion which was just that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could turn, please, to paragraphs 34 and 35. And perhaps that can be displayed in Sanction, sufficiently redacted. I want to ask you about what's in paragraph 34, but referable back to paragraph -- sorry, 35 but referable back to -- referable back to 34, where you said that: "This was the last time that (redacted) were allowed access to KLA-controlled territories in Decani municipality. One of our researchers told me in April 1998, while heading to Glodjane the researcher was stopped at a KLA check-point in Pozar and that Daut Haradinaj himself refused to allow the researcher to proceed." Are you able to give the Trial Chamber any more information about that? And that is contained in that passage in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. Again, just the context of these events. The last ten days of April there was a clash between KLA and police forces. Refugees -- Albanian refugees were fleeing toward Djakovica from Erec, if I remember well, while Serbian refugees were, like, heading -- the rest would stay there, heading towards youth hotels behind Decani monastery, and we all tried as a team to basically interview refugees and find out what's happening. And that was the moment when one of the researchers went -- tried to see what's happening with Albanian refugees and enter the check-point in Pozar and was refused to enter further.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, in that passage in your statement, you referred to access to KLA-controlled territories in Decani municipality. Which areas were then, as far as you could see, KLA-controlled?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had some information that KLA controlled Babaloc, Shaptej, Gramocelj, Dubrava, while Serbian police forces being in a settlement of Babaloc for a while and also in Agro-Combinat behind for a while. In that period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one thing to clarify. You make a distinction between Babaloc and Babaloc -- the settlement of Babaloc. By "the settlement of Babaloc," you mean the newly built, I would say, street -- streets, et cetera, and some 50 or 80 newly built houses for refugees. Is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one matter, if I might. When the witness indicates at page 4, line 7 "that period of time," I wonder if we might clarify whether she's referring to the period of time she's describing in paragraphs 34 and 35 of her witness statement or some other period of time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the period from Easter, which was 19th of April, to 30th -- 30th of April, probably. After that, I'm not aware, because I was not there any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the source of your information about the KLA controlling the areas you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have difficulties remembering that now, but I think it was in Djakovica the committee for protection of human rights, because we usually relied on them to go and get the basic facts what's happening with the -- on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In Spotlight Report 26, which is Exhibit P6 - and you have a copy there in front of you - I think it's at page 17, the report refers to -- this is 00649633, ERN. Under the heading at 9: "Glodjane controlled by liberation army of Kosovo," it says: "Following the 24th of March clash, the Liberation Army of Kosovo (LAK) set up check-points at the entrance and exit of Glodjane and barred news reporters from the village." Is that passage in that report to which you contributed and your incident reports were used to compile referable to the part in paragraph 35 where you say that one of your researchers was stopped from entering Glodjane in April 1998? Is there a connection between the two, the barring of (redacted) and the barring of news reporters from Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not connect these two -- two facts. I had many connection with the media, and also media reported a lot about different attempts of -- to enter that space. So I am not sure this connects at all to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please turn to page -- sorry, paragraph 40 of your statement in relation to the Babaloc refugee settlement. And you mentioned Babaloc a moment ago. And if paragraph 40 could just be displayed in Sanction there. "In April 1998, I interviewed two refugees from a settlement." And you've got their names. "They told me that on the evening of the 18th of April 1998, the KLA had attacked the house of Zarko Zlaticanin. The house was hit but nobody was hurt. The following day many of the refugees left for Podgorica." What did they tell you about the attack on the night of 18th of April, 1998? Describe what they told you about the attack.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite difficult to recollect everything what they said. I remember me being with a little bit -- having mistrusts towards them, because they insisted there was no police force there, they were just coming to visit them. And I just arrived from Albanian villages in, I think, Skivije, where Albanian refugees were insisting the police forces were there. So one of the reasons I went there was actually to check what is happening. But they said that on 18th, so in the eve of the Easter, shooting came from the village of Babaloc, which -- because that -- if I understand and as I could remember, there is some forest and split between Albanian village of Babaloc and the settlement of Babaloc. They said also that these attacks were also happening in 1997 but not so frequent. 18th started seriously shooting from Suka e Baballoq, they said, and that Albanians were shouting, "Happy Easter." That shooting continued on 19th and that 19th in the afternoon they -- they were kind of doing nothing, hiding. They've been escorted to Decani youth hostel. And then returned back, I think, on 20th, which told me - maybe I was wrong to conclude - that in the meantime Serbian police forces retook the position, because Albanian refugees were talking about Suka e Babaloc and Suka Crmljanska is the position of the Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Excuse me. I apologise for interrupting again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I wonder if that passage, which I slightly lost the sense of, could -- could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 28, I think Mr. Emmerson did not exactly understand what you meant, I take it especially from where you said that you may have drawn wrong conclusions. Could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I -- it's just my conclusion because of the dates that all these events were happening. Because I -- I am in the same time also in Albanian villages with Albanian refugees, and they are saying that on 20th basically they had to leave and ran away from, I think, Erec, because Serbian police forces start controlling Suka e Babaloc and Suka Crmljanska and start shooting at them. The same time the Serbian refugees in the settlement of Babaloc saying that on 18th and 19th was actually attacked by KLA on them. So my conclusion was that we had a conflict, that there were refugees fleeing in different directions to avoid it. I don't know if that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings me to another question. Earlier you testified that -- where you said "the last ten days of April there was a clash between KLA and police forces, refugees, Albanian refugees were fleeing towards Djakovica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if you remember it well, Serbian refugees were heading, I think, towards the youth hostel behind Decani. What I'd like to ask you is: On -- on the basis of the information received and on the basis of you -- what you observed yourself, was it that Serbs were fleeing when KLA attacks took place? Was it that Albanians were fleeing when Serbian attacks took place? Or was it that there was armed conflict where it was not easy to identify who was attacking and who was defending but just exchange of fire, violence, where the whole of the population, irrespective of who was shooting or who was attacking, just got out of their villages in order to protect themselves? Or was it -- I hope you understand my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it was a specific response, fleeing, from a specific attack, or whether it was widespread violence, including several forces, where -- whether you were Serbian or whether you were Albanian you'd leave the territory because it would become too dangerous for all of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't have an impression that was kind of uncontrolled and wide and unknown attackers behind, especially with the Babaloc settlement refugees, because they clearly pointed toward Babaloc village, Albanian village, saying that they are shooting them and they are pulling out and with the escort of police hardly could reach youth hostel there. The same thing happened with the Albanian refugees. They were saying that Serbian police is actually in certain positions shelling the villages and because of that they were running. That's what I can recollect now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's not -- you didn't gain the impression that where people were fleeing for violence, that they were perhaps misinterpreting the situation, blaming the violence necessarily to what were their natural opponents, that is, Albanians for the Serbs and Serbs for the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I had impression is that they both, of course, insisted they've been unarmed. So Serbs are saying that they -- they haven't been armed and they just without any weapons were sitting there in the settlement, which actually Albanians said differently. And also Albanian refugees were insisting that men stayed behind and that they are all civilians guarding their homes. But my feeling was at that point that it was already established some kind of -- two -- two different military groups, one against the other, one very weak, like KLA, not very -- probably well-armed but kind of ready to fight and more powerful Serbian police forces that basically wanted to keep that road open between Decani and Djakovica. I think everything was at these ten days about the road between Decani and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to the section in your statement from paragraph 44 down: "Serb families living in Dukagjini area in early 1998." If that could be displayed in Sanction, please, the rest of that page. Now, in the middle of the first paragraph - this is 44 - you say: "We received information that some Serb civilians in Albanian villages had been kidnapped by the KLA and were missing." You then go down -- two sentences down to say: "(redacted) decided to investigate the accuracy of the claims, and I arrived in Decani in the last week of April 1998 to investigate." Next paragraph: "In Decani, I counted 34 Serb families who had left their villages in the Dukagjini area and were living in Decani as refugees." I want to concentrate on that. Firstly, how did you calculate the figure of 34 families in that sentence and 123 in the next sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 123, I have to say, I really don't know the source. I knew that I had that in my notebook, 123 numbers stays in my head. I can't recollect what is the source for that number. For these 34 families I did count them and I will tell you how. First maybe it's worth mentioning that these families were not unknown to us. We'd been receiving reports from early March that those -- some of those families were attacked, some were already leaving, and our researcher, who still could go in March, Serbian researcher, was interviewing these families. So I knew -- I was familiar with those families. When I arrived there, what I usually did in that time was I draw the map. These villages were not totally known to me, and I draw the map with the villages and I concentrated on the right side of the road looking from Djakovica to Decani; meaning that would be east -- yeah, east -- east side of the road. And then I didn't, of course, calculate every single person there. I wish I could. But what I did, I put down the numbers of the houses, families. Serbs in those villages were similarly organised as families in Albanian families, meaning, say, three families of Popovic, five families -- five houses -- five houses of Stojanovic, three houses there. So that's the -- the way how I did it. And I paid attention specifically, because media in Serbia, Russian media in Serbia were, I thought, exaggerating the numbers and talking about hundreds of families being expelled. And maybe it's interesting to mention here that five families from Gramocelj, Albanian families from Gramocelj, I was told - I didn't see them - but I was told were there who didn't want to take the arms. And that's how I then later -- out of this, actually, listing the families created a lot of confusion later because some names and the families were mysteriously later not being able to track. We prepared that report later, so I tried to find some of them. And some of these missing had different surnames. For example, these two old ladies, one handicapped, Serbs there in Decani told me that they are Vujorad Dara [phoen], Ante Vujosevic, but in reality later I realised that one was married and was Kovac, or something like that. But I had them as Vujosevic in my list. Am I actually talking too much answering the questions that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. No, you're trying to clearly explain what Mr. Re asks you. And if you would enter any area where Mr. Re thinks that we should focus on other areas, he'll certainly then interrupt you. And -- and if we have the same feeling, we'll do the same.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can I just take you back to your last answer. And you said that "we were -- we'd been receiving reports from early March that some of those families were attacked, some were already leaving." What were the reports you'd been receiving? What were the nature of the attacks? What had you been told about the attacks on these families? That is, who had been attacking them? In what manner? And what was the result of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember all family names that we then interviewed, especially that was done by other researchers, so I can't -- and I don't have an insight into regional statements there that stated "(redacted) (redacted)." I remember some names and some villages that they came from. And I know that it was the beginning of the March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the names and the villages you can remember and what you were told about the nature of the attacks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I -- I remember from some family Fatic from Crmljane that was -- bomb was thrown into their yard. A similar thing was in Culafic. I think it was Ratis. That's what I'm not sure. There was the Bozanic family, a Montenegrin family in Rznic, and for them I know that I tried to track them later but -- and I heard that there their son lives in Belgrade and they moved immediately after clash in Glodjane there. Was that -- one more? I can't remember any more. I might actually remember later that last name of that fourth family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from the name, do you remember the -- the place and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no one hurt, as far as I remember. We just got -- we seen reports in Serbian media that these Serbian houses were attacked. So our researcher went there, interviewed them, and got a different material about bombs being there. Mostly bombs, I remember, being thrown in their yards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the information about who had put the bombs in their yards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that really. I can't remember. To me, because I followed the development KLA from the before and from Dreznica, was quite -- I had already some information about KLA being there, so that was logical. But I can't say it was KLA, because I don't see these interviews any more. But what I remember now is curfew that existed beginning of 1998, and I remember specific interview that was made by one researcher -- researcher, Serbian, with a family that was stopped explicitly by KLA. And a car was shot. Nobody was hurt. And I think they even have that interview somewhere with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember -- where you said "beginning of 1998," could you be more specific as far as month is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was actually some kind of saint. The end of December. And they were traveling to monastery. Which monastery, I don't know any more. And they were stopped on that road and they'd been interviewed by the Serbian researcher and explained that they didn't know for curfew but all other Serbs knew, and that was the case, I remember. I mean, I might find actually that interview, if -- if it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you mean that -- the end of December 1997?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And you referred to the curfew. What was the curfew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The curfew was related to some -- that KLA was patrolling and then they couldn't go out from the houses. And then there was one more family, I think, but that was not in that -- that was not in Decani. It was in Klina. That they'd been saying -- Donji Petrovic [phoen] in Klina. They'd been saying that they took the weapons and they were guarding their house -- Serbian house, fearing of the KLA attacks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was March.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where was this incident of the shooting of the car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Josanica. I think something like Josanica. Turici or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should be further near Klina. Norther than -- north from Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The border maybe with the -- with the Drenica region.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And the curfew. Were you saying the KLA imposed the curfew or someone else imposed the curfew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA imposed the curfew. That was in that interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Now, these abductions of ethnic -- of ethnic Serbs are referred to in the Human Rights Watch report "Violations of the rules -- humanitarian law violations in Kosovo." That's 65 ter Exhibit number 999. If you turn to pages 78 and 79, where at the footnote its sources for some of the information about the abductions of ethnic Serbs is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this already in evidence, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No. But I'm going to ask for it to be -- to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I see it's quite a -- a long report. Do you need everything of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, yes. It's a -- it's a report which is of the period from -- all through 1998 and is a balance report referring to what was happening on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I may, in the event that the Prosecution is going to be seeking to tender this particular exhibit, we're going to be objecting to it based on the ruling in the Milutinovic case concerning these kinds of documents. And we're happy to make further written submissions about it at a later point in time, but I just want to set a marker at this time with regard to this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, then reports summarising the whole of the conflict are at least problematic, so I would encourage you to -- first of all, to focus on those portions you would specifically like to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's -- it's directly relevant to the incidents which are in the indictment. It refers to a number of the people who were listed in the indictment. That's the preliminary step I'm taking with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Witness 28, I just want you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether it's relevance that's at the basis of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, there are going to be -- there are going to be actually a series of objections with regard to this particular kind of evidence. Perhaps what would be the most prudent thing would be to file a written submission. But I -- and ask at this point for the Chamber to withhold any ruling with regard to the admission of this particular document. I just wanted to alert the Chamber to the fact that we would be following the reasoning in the decision of the 1st of September, 2006 concerning evidence tendered through Sandra Mitchell and Frederick Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Which I believe also has applicable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, you are aware that this is, I would say, that this is a repeating issue to what extent summarising evidence by others could be admitted, because I take it that you want to have it admitted since -- to establish the content of the report as being the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. And also for the conclusion which Human Rights Watch came to in relation to when the conflict occurred and the intensity and level of it based upon their experiences on the ground, and that's at pages 91 to 93. And I've referred to that in -- but could -- would it be possible just to have it marked for identification now and have this debate at a later point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, of course, once the witness has concluded testimony, then of course if we have not or only very partially admit this into evidence, then of course you're facing the problem that where you thought that quite a lot of material would be in evidence, that it might not be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, that's not what where I'm coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I want to do is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll MFI it for --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want her to identify the certain passages as linking back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's all I want to take up with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has yet seen the witness statement of -- I'm sure there's no application for protective measures, but if I get it wrong -- no, I see there isn't -- of Peter Bouckaert of Human Rights Watch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Fred Abrahams.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Fred Abrahams of Human Rights Watch who produces this report as well or refers to this report as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we don't have -- we haven't seen it. Which doesn't mean that we are not aware of it coming in our direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. We know that -- just apropos the point Mr. Re makes moment ago, there are very considerable passages of that statement which objection is going to be taken, including and perhaps in particular the conclusion that Mr. Re adverts to is the appropriate date for the start of an armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at least this report, Human Rights Watch report, receives an MFI number. And that would be, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be marked for identification as P1212.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All I want to do you, Witness 28, is for you to identify some sections in this report, Human Rights Watch report, which are referable to the work you and (redacted) did in Kosovo in 1998. And the first one is at pages 78 to 79, which refers to the abduction of ethnic Serbs. And paragraph -- and footnote 134 and 138 actually refer -- actually footnote to (redacted) reports. I just want you to confirm that that is -- that is in fact the case. And then I want to take you to another passage in it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you could just turn to the specific incidents at paragraph 49 -- sorry, 48, where you say you interviewed some of the refugees in Decan; then paragraph 49. If that could -- also could be displayed in Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm lost now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Paragraph 49, where you refer to an interview with Milovan and Milka Vlahovic's daughter, Nada Vlahovic. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And thereafter on the page in paragraph 51, where you refer to "The refugees telling me that the only Serbs remaining in Dasinovac were Slobodan Milosevic, Milica Radunovic, Milos Radunovic, and the Markovic family." Now, firstly I just want you to refer to you to page 83 of MFI P1212, which is the Human Rights Watch report. And the footnote of 149 refers to (redacted) report, which is in Exhibit P6 -- or P5, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And is it fair to say the Human Rights Watch report bases its information on information which (redacted) --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- obtained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And if you could just turn over to the next page, which is page 84 of the Human Rights Watch report, where it says: "According to the (redacted) and newspaper Blic, Gurum Bejta [phoen] and Agron Berisa, both Roma, and Ivan Zaric, an ethnic Serb, left Dolac on May 20th for the villages of Grabovica. As of August 1999 their whereabouts were unknown." Again -- that's footnote 151 -- is that also information the Human Rights Watch is basing upon that newspaper report and the information which your research has gathered on the ground in Kosovo at the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to now take you to -- sorry, paragraph 50. In the middle of it it says: "Nada Vlahovic told me that Serbs -- that when the Serbs were leaving, the Albanian families also left the village. Only the Albanian men stayed behind. My experience was that this was a typical and normal occurrence in villages where the KLA appeared in public. The Albanian women and children would leave the village as well fearing clashes between the KLA, MUP, or VJ." Now, can you just briefly tell the Trial Chamber what your experience was of that and how you were able to come to that conclusion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My experience was that Serbian police forces were absolutely without control once getting into the clashes or entering the villages where they suspected of being attacked by KLA, which then meant that Albanian villagers tried to save the children and the women and send them further as possible so that they cannot -- save their lives. And that was one vicious circle, I would say, which I don't know who should be blamed really on the end of the day, because Serbian police also shouldn't, I think, exaggerate the level of the attacks and make -- creating new waves of the refugees, basically. At a certain point in the summer it became really chaos. But yes, that's true that mostly Serbs would tell -- tell us, I think Nada Vlahovic, but also that Ljubica Stojanovic, that, for example, before Glodjane clashes on 24th of March, they noticed that some Albanian families left the village. And sometimes also Albanian women said that their men stayed behind to look for the house. So it's fear, fear that clashes would occur and somebody would get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could take you now to paragraph 53. If that could also be displayed in Sanction, where you say: "Some Serb refugees staying in the youth hostel in Decani told me that a Serb from Prilep, Branko Stamatovic disappeared on the 25th of April, 1998." Do you have any further information on that? If not, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we had in one report that, I'm not sure if I can remember, there was one Albanian source telling us that Branko was seen entering with the Serbian police somebody's house or something like that, but I'm not sure that this man is alive any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could turn to the next paragraph, 54, under the heading "Conditions along the main roads in mid-1998," where you say: "My observations from traveling in the -- frequently in the Dukagjini area from March 1999" -- I'm sorry, 1998 -- I'll say it again. "March 1998 onwards was of an escalation of the conflict." Would you describe to the Trial Chamber this escalation of the conflict you observed from March 1998 -- 1998 onwards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from March I don't remember seeing any police check-points in such a big numbers. Roads were open. Buses still worked, although some of them were stopped and some people kidnapped out of the buses. That changed quite a lot. Again, I am talking about these ten days of April, last April where buses stopped work. There were a lot of check-points. Many Albanian refugees testified that they could see convoys, police and military convoys on -- on the road, especially between Decani-Djakovica. I also heard that behind the monastery arrived special Serbian forces and from other side Albanian refugees were calling that part Podi i Geshtenjave, I think that's the part how it was called, where they settled there. So there was a tension growing and more refugees coming. Another point is there is a border where very often media were reporting about Yugoslav Army stopping the convoys with the -- not convoys but basically people -- arresting people with weapons, carrying through the borders. And then I think that a lot of refugees from Voksh or -- what's called that? Another place. Was heading toward Djakovica again, from the other side toward Djakovica. Fearing the clashes are already maybe happening, the clashes. I can't remember that. But yes, the roads were becoming the problem. The roads in April quite a bit. In May actually almost very difficult to travel on that road to Djakovica from Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what was it about the conflict you saw escalating? That's what I'm specifically getting to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I was not the -- a witness of the conflict. I could just put together the bits and pieces of information I got, and I also was worried where to send researchers, not to send a Serbian researcher in KLA-controlled zone or not to sentence Albanian researchers over the check-points of the Serbs, who were quite angry. And so I was monitoring that process, and I -- I could see very nervous check-points, Serbian policemen, behind the sandbags, struggling to keep the road open, insisting that basically KLA is going to close the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In paragraph 65, you refer to an incident on the 24th or 25th of May when you were driving (redacted) jeep to Pec or Peja with your team to abuse -- to investigate abuses in Serbian police custody. And at the bottom of the paragraph, you said: "We heard that the KLA had also kidnapped two police near Prilep on the Decani-Djakovica road." I just want to cross-reference that. Is that -- if you could turn to Spotlight Report number 27, which is part of P6. If you could go to paragraph 2.24, which is at page K0078707. It refers to the abduction of police officers Nikola Jovanovic and Rade Popovic. Is that the same incident to which you're referring in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is but we didn't investigate that -- in the incident that was taken, as I remember, from media. I just heard that there was something else happening of the road, not just Ljubenic attack but also something else just happened or happened day before. I can't remember any more. And then I also heard there were related to that case that there are some negotiations. If true, that these policemen to be released. But it failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you could turn to paragraph 75, please. If that could also be displayed in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Just in respect of the last line of the last answer. I wonder if the witness could give the source for that, please. The reference to negotiations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I think it was daily -- daily newspaper, Danas. But we have it here, I think, mentioned in this document that he was referring to. Can you help me to find that paragraph here? Can you help me? This is about that Poparic -- Nikola Ivanic case. Poparic. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. This may be -- oh, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 224, it reads: "The paper further reported that there had been contacts between the police authorities and the KLA."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- "on exchanging captured police officers in return for food supplies." Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from what the papers reported, you have no additional information --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- apart from this was reported.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Because this report was made partly based on what we researched and partly on what local media reported. And we stated -- quoted the sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If we could go to paragraph 75, which is displayed in Sanction there. You refer to the Serbian media (redacted) documenting "increased KLA attacks on MUP patrols on the Djakovica-Decani-Pec road (including the kidnapping and killing of police and civilians).". You then refer to your assessment saying: "Based upon my field research, my assessment was that they in turn provoked retaliation by the MUP. The MUP then retaliated by the indiscriminate shelling and burning of Albanian villages." Then you go down: "Resulting in an exodus of Albanian women and children. Meanwhile Albanian male villagers were being mobilised. The MUP retaliation in May 1998 seemed to be specifically targeted at places like Decani and Ljubenic, but in summer spread across all of Kosovo. The MUP needed control the towns and main roads." What -- I just want you to elaborate on that, the MUP needed to control the towns and the main roads. What was your information about the control in the Dukagjini area in May 1998? ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this is really now opinion. It is not based on any special information. The fact -- pure fact that there was a road that was dividing basically western side -- yeah, eastern side of -- of the road with the villages by then controlled by the end of May by KLA, I think. And then also the border where the -- the weapons was coming was quite clearly the way that -- that was the intention, to have territory and open the way for the weapons to come in. And the Serbs, just not only in case of Decani but also in Orahovac or anywhere else, whenever somebody would try to close the road or somebody would try to take the town under control, they just didn't let it happen. Nothing more I can say that. It was just my assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I want to just take you back to an answer you gave before to Judge Orie when he was asking you about people fleeing the violence in March and April 1998.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you able to determine from your interviews and your observations in the field a pattern to what the Albanians or Serbs were telling (redacted)?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean specifically for that region? Because we covered all Kosovo. Are you asking for Decani?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That region, yes, Decani, Dukagjini.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Serbs actually had expressed pure belief that they're targeted and they're -- they were told to leave the houses. Sometimes then they feared that they would be targeted. There was a lot -- different reports about some foreign armies, as they would call, in Decani area. So some of them actually were arrested and beaten, as I understand, in KLA headquarter in Glodjane. Albanians from other side were actually saying almost always the same, "The Serbian forces are on this Suka e Babaloc and Suka Crmljanska," and they are showing them that's the reason why they are leaving. Both sides insisted they are not armed, that we interviewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who was -- what was your information about who was targeting the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you ask the Serbs then, they would all have -- say just a couple of expressions. They would say "Siptari", terrorists, "OVK," "UCK." These are the expressions that they've been using all the time. However, I have to say that Serbian media were so much in propaganda against the terrorists that we started actually worrying a certain point, I think actually after March, that we don't actually see how this is developing. If everything the Serbs says OVK -- or terrorists did this. That's why we then tried to basically identify have they been actually armed or they had weapons or they've been under uniform, in uniforms, or just it's opinion that they are terrorists who are attacking you, or rather, them. Maybe it's important to say political element into this terminology. I don't know if it's -- maybe important, maybe not. But Serbs for a while didn't want to admit that they have actually military conflict and wanted to have that perception that they are honest Albanians and some terrorists and gangs roaming around. I think for a while also LDK of Kosovo for, like, beginning of the clashes -- beginning of the -- what I see as the war, also didn't want to admit that KLA exists, so that was -- that's why Serbs mostly used "terrorists," "terrorists," "terrorists," but also "OVK," "KLA," "UCK" also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just going back to your observations and what you were able to verify and determine based on interviews and what you saw on the roads, was it more consistent with the existence of the KLA targeting the Serb families or was it consistent with something else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I didn't understand this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shall we -- if the witness doesn't understand the question, then another question or a rephrased question should be put to her. Once the question is there, Mr. Emmerson, I take it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think more generally -- I haven't interrupted up until now. As we've been drifting further and further away from specifics and more and more into generalisations and assessments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But I think, if I may say so, we're well beyond proper bounds by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- you've described propaganda in the media, what the Serb -- who had left -- who had left their villages and said they'd been targeted had said to you. You've described -- your statement says you were in Kosovo in that area at the time observing movements and things happening on the road. Based on everything you saw, what -- what was -- what was -- what was -- what the Serbs were saying to you was consistent with what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see whether we can resolve the matter. You said earlier - and I'll find the passage - you said that the Serbs didn't want to admit that KLA exists. That's why Serbs mostly used "terrorists," terrorists" -- but also and then a few other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, do I understand your answer well that you consider this to be unrealistic, saying that -- or not wanting to admit that KLA existed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. I actually think that KLA existed then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when for the first time you noticed for yourself that the denial of the existence of KLA was unrealistic? When for the first time you thought, what they are doing is unrealistic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean Serbian?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, immediately after Likosane event that I mentioned on Thursday evening. Because it is obvious that there is a popular uprising after that. Then I talked to some sources in LDK and I was told that already are groups on the ground not still army. It was February 1998. And not still army but people are just flooding to support them. Albanians really had been disappointed that the issue was not sorted out after Dayton and start actually getting into a position to look at this process of peaceful maintaining process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So that's what I thought. Prekaz, again, the next big massacre that happened on 5th or 6th. Again, I think, recruitment of the people. So there is genuine movement behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you say Serbs denied KLA to exist. I understand KLA to be Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time, you say in February 1998 and not still army. When for the first time, then, it came into your mind that a denial of the existence of an army was not consistent with what you considered to be an army? And I'll then later ask you why you considered at a certain moment where you said in February "not still army," then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not me. The source in the LDK told me this is still not the army, but it's having the support, widespread support. We are a little worried. But if I thought a month ago that it would not be the war, now I cannot say it any more. So that's what somebody else told me. I -- I'm not military expert. I just saw actually KLA -- yeah, KLA soldiers. I seen them in Prekaz. I seen them in Cirez and Likosane. I also had passed in -- outside Dreznica, had some contacts with commanders there. So I was aware that it was army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you told us this, you're referring not only to the Dukagjini area but the wider area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, the wider area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Re, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then -- three Defence counsels. Who's going first? Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think that's the plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 28, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Emmerson, who's counsel for Mr. Haradinaj. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, please, Witness 28 to turn to paragraph 65 of your witness statement. There's just one preliminary topic I want to cover with you, if I may. In paragraph 65, the opening lines of that paragraph indicate that on the 24th or 25th of May, you were driving with your team to investigate abuses in Serbian police custody, to speak to lawyers and local Albanian human rights workers. Now, you go on in your statement to explain that when you arrived in Pec you heard about incidents that had occurred in Dolovo and Ljubenic, which I'm going to come back to. But I want to ask --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one thing. I am quite -- I thought a lot. There are a place -- two places. One is called Dolovo, one is called Dolac. And they're all along the road Klina. I'm not sure is that Dolovo or Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Well, we'll -- we'll --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We'll come back to the Ljubenic dimension in a little while. But what I want to ask you about, please, is the investigation that you were then conducting and what, if anything, it led to. I want to ask you what inquiries you made during that investigation into abuse of Albanian prisoners detained by Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the intention, the real intention why we went there? We actually gave up the same second of that, because we already heard that Ljubenic is problem, so Albanian researchers immediately day after went into Ljubenic, and Serbian researcher that day went to find somebody who was wounded, I think in this case, in front of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. So that -- that mission to investigate --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- abuse was abandoned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Did you ever pick that project up again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a project. Let me clarify. What we really did - and I think it's to appraise all the team - we've been actually every morning reading newspapers and seeing especially KIC, which is Kosovo Information Centre. And we would get out of that many, many, many different names of abuse and torture and prison. So this, what was happening with the Serbs was like 1 per cent of our work. Everything else was dealing with the -- basically widespread abuse of Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I can't say that specific project. The project was ongoing daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. If we could look at paragraph 26 of your statement for a moment. You assert there in the first sentence that it was: "Well known that a culture of corruption existed at all levels within the law enforcement and judicial systems in Kosovo." And then a little further down at the bottom end of the paragraph, you refer to the practice of what are known as informative talks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And you say: "That was the normal expression then used by Serbian police when they intended to beat or torture persons in order to extract information or confessions."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, to explain the basis for those two assertions, what it is that you base those on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Informative discussions were something not only present in Kosovo. I was personally invited a couple of times for informative discussions. And that meant not really just informing but in -- by many Albanians who actually told me that, meant really beating and torturing people in the prison. But then out of that, some of the Serbian command structures basically made money, so they said, Well, let's charge it. And sometimes they pretended, and sometimes not. But it was quite a financially successful job.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: In paragraph 34 of your statement, when dealing with the aftermath of the incident in Gllogjan on the 24th of March, you say that you received reports that many local Albanians were arrested and taken to the Decani police station, where they were interrogated and beaten. And my first question is: What was the source of those reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source were Albanian witnesses of the event, and that were police intervention in Glodjane. Because we had Albanian researchers interviewing witnesses of the event. And as far as I remember there, was also a school where the children were scared and the parents tried to save the children there. I also think that Serbian police at certain point used some men, Albanian, as cover -- as hostages or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: These reports that you received --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- of Albanians being beaten during interrogation --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- were they unique or were they typical of information that you received about the treatment of Albanian suspects in Serb police custody in Western Kosovo at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was typical across the Kosovo, not only Western Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Are you able to give any more information about that practice, if it was a practice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'm sure that you can find at (redacted) many, many, many interviews that we made with the people who were beaten or tortured, especially after Orahovac fell. I remember that I talked actually with some people, Albanians -- not some; many -- who were later taken to Stimlje or somewhere -- Prizren in the police station and some, I think, were killed. For some people, I know that they were killed in prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We're going to see with you in a moment if I can just trace that observation through with you. But could we look, please, just briefly at the report that Mr. Re has just taken you to and this has just been marked for identification, the humanitarian law violations in Kosovo report. And I ask these questions, if I may, without prejudice to the submissions about admissibility of this document. And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I have this -- that on my screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to ask you, please -- it's P1212, and it's page 53 of the document I want to ask you about. Sorry, page -- I think we have page 45. It's -- it should be page 53. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Under the heading "Arrests -- detentions and arrests," the document records in the first sentence that arbitrary detentions and arrests of ethnic Albanians have escalated rapidly throughout 1998. And then if I can just drop down to the next paragraph: "In July and August, detained individuals increasingly included human rights activists, humanitarian aid workers, political party members, doctors, and lawyers, many of whom were physically abused in custody Human Rights Watch has substantial and credible evidence from lawyers and family members of detainees that torture and ill-treatment" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, you're reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: "That torture and ill-treatment of detainees is common, especially in the police stations during the first days in custody. From March to August 1998, five people" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Too fast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're now just finished the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm following the transcript without listening to the translation. It's the usual error.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If I can pick it up then. "From March to August 1998, five people are known to have died from torture while in police custody; hundreds of others have been beaten." And then there's a reference to restricted access. Then at the very bottom of that section there, are two lines that read: "In the past, terrorist-related trials have been marred by serious procedural irregularities, as well as the use of torture to extract confessions." I want you to help us, if you can, please, as to what you know of that practice and whether you have information as to whether it was a systematic practice or not.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a systematic practice. Exactly the lawyers that they are mentioned here, I had quite well-established lawyers, contacts with the lawyers, so they've been the source of serious cases and informations to (redacted) had own lawyer who was following just because of that different procedures so we could somehow warn public if something like that is happening. But yes, it was quite often and systematic. My understanding was that witnessing, I don't know, maybe -- maybe that's a history then and it's not important, but in 1996 and 1997 there were a lot of attacks on different targets, usually police forces and sometimes loyal Albanians. And KLA was taking, actually for public statements possibility for this. And somehow it was a circle, they would then enter the house and arrest everybody in relation and then torture all family to extract some -- some of this -- to admit that they are terrorists and that would make more terrorists coming through.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I want -- in the context of this specific research done by the (redacted), please, to look with you at a document which has been marked for identification as D194. And I'm going to go to specific passages of it, and so might I ask that this small bundle of documents be handed around. The document, the extract of which is behind tab 2 in this bundle, is D194, and it's a (redacted) report authored by Natasa Kandic and dated November 2001 but relating to events during 1998 and 1999. And I wonder -- could I ask you behind tab 2A -- I'm sorry, behind tab 2B to look at page 12, first of all. And just about two-thirds of the way down the page, the last full paragraph before the quotation, it reads: "Torture was systematically applied towards the detained ethnic Albanian citizens. They were subjected to most severe methods of physical and psychological maltreatment and cruel, inhumane, and degrading treatment during the time -- entire time of their detention." And there's then a reference to the conditions in which people were held, with denial of medical help, medicine, food, and drink. And it goes on: "They were inhumanly and cruelly punished by being tied to a light-post, beaten with batons, with electrical -- electric and baseball bats, including torture by using electric shocks." And then there's a reference to a list of individuals for who there was a serious indication that they had died in detention as a consequence of torture. Now, is that the group of individuals that you were referring to earlier on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's -- as I remember -- but I am familiar with these names, except for one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rexhep Musaku, I don't remember that name. This is Uvisevac [phoen] case. Trials monitored with a separate department with (redacted), but we also as the researchers were interviewing actually family members, how they were arrested and, what was happening. Concretely, I recognise the names. I don't know the details, except Rexhep Musaku case, name I don't recognise.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Based on the interviews you were conducting during your time in Kosovo, do you agree with the conclusion that torture was systematically applied?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we could just turn to paragraph 20, please -- I'm sorry, page 20, paragraph 2.1. Again, by reference to statements taken by (redacted). At the bottom of that page is a paragraph which reads as follows: "The detained Albanians faced hours of maltreatment so that they would admit an act, sign some statement, i.e. so that they would repeat the story to the investigative judge, a story that had been extorted from them by the MUP organs. Before an accused was taken to the investigative judge, the MUP members combined their methods of violence (by beating with batons, draining with hunger, thirst, and sleeplessness) by threats and blackmail, so as to 'form' the prisoner's statement." And then there's an example: "Faik Hoti was told that he would 'be killed completely', while Danush Kurtaj was told that he would be tortured when he returns from the investigative judge if he changes the statement he confirmed to the police." My first question is: Does that summary information accurately reflect information given to you from lawyers that you interviewed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And secondly, this, we've heard some evidence --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although, this case is coming from the period where I already haven't been there, but it does reflect --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can we just clarify this. It appears from my reading of this report it that relates to events either in 1999 or to places outside the indictment area. If Mr. Emmerson could clarify that, I'd be satisfied by where it's going.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's a series of specific examples given, some of them inside the indictment area, some of them outside. For example, there was an 1999 example in May from the municipality of Pec. And there are certainly examples within the interviews of allegations made during the indictment period. But the questions that I'm putting to the witness are based on the interviews that she conducted whether the conclusions in the report are consistent with the information that she was obtaining from detained Albanians and their lawyers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, I think it -- that clarifies. But, of course, if it's consistent with events that took place later, then, of course, it might not be of any relevance, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps I should clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was this consistent with information that was provided to you about detentions during 1998?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I still object. That still doesn't make it relevant. The fact that (redacted) report refers to things in 1999 doesn't -- it can't make it relevant for some things the Serbs might have done in 1998 in the indictment area. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- further, what is the relevance to the allegations before the Court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, what -- as far as I understand, Mr. Emmerson is now asking, but -- is whether the information which we find in the report to some extent covering the indictment period, to some extent outside the indictment period, whether that was consistent with the information that was provided to you by the detentions during 1998. I think the 1998 detentions are important, what happened later on could --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Exactly so. Which is why I'm not relying on the interviews themselves but on the witness's testimony that what is here reflected --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then please focus on what in the interviews the witness held was said about detention in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Let me just, for the sake of absolute clarity, put the position to you specifically: From interviews carried out by you and your organisation with detained Albanians and their lawyers, was it -- was it a common occurrence that it would be reported to you that torture was practiced?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Was it so common as to be capable, in your judgement, of being described as "systematic"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And that would have covered the whole of Kosovo, including the Dukagjin area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly -- mostly after the -- when arrests happened, after the summer clashes between the KLA and police forces. Then there would be systematic arrests of the people and then whoever was arrested was tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you noticed similar allegation between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- could we first ask: When you are talking about the summer clashes, you are referring to the summer 1998 clashes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1998, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: But you recorded yourself within your organisation similar allegations being made has early as the 24th of March following those clashes in Gllojane?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1997 also.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, referring to the passage I just took you to, there was a record there of individual -- of an individual being threatened that unless he repeated before the investigating judge a statement that had been beaten from him in police custody, he would be beaten when he returns from the investigative judge. Now, I just want to ask if you can help us with that a little. We've heard some testimony in this court that once a person has been brought before the investigative judge they would not be returned to the custody of the MUP but would be returned to a form of investigative detention so that they could not thereafter be beaten by the officers who may have used force to extract their confession.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can you help us as to whether that's accurate or not, from the system as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that at the moment when I worked there, my job was just to somehow coordinate and cover events, events, events. And the -- all monitoring of the trials. I was updated as it -- the time goes, but I didn't really follow the trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I just have that kind of knowledge listening my colleagues, lawyers, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And based on your conversation with your colleagues and lawyers, were there allegations of people being threatened by the MUP that unless they repeated their statements before the investigative judge they would be beaten afterwards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was typical.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And, again, are you able to comment on the suggestion that it wouldn't be possible for the MUP to beat a suspect after he or she had appeared before the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see the time. Would this be a convenient moment to take a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would be a convenient moment. Could I, at the same time, inquire into the time Defence counsel expect still to need.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I have quite a considerable amount of material to cover with this witness. Might I give Your Honour an accurate time estimate when we return?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a break until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start. Mr. Emmerson, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, just to turn to paragraph 46 of your witness statement once again very briefly, where you are referring to some interviews that were conducted with Serb families in Decani. I just want to ask you this. You say: "we interviewed as many refugees as we could." When you say "we interviewed" -- It may be just wise if we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I may be overcautious but ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I just want to see if I've understood the evidence that you've given so far in -- in connection with armed incidents in the area of Baballoq in April correctly. If we could start, please, with paragraph 42 of your statement. You say there that as far as you could recall at that time, that is, the 28th of April, there was no MUP station based in the settlement, although you had information from refugees that the MUP were patrolling regularly. And then you say, rather -- in connection with your interviews of Albanian refugees, that they insisted that the police was shooting at them from Suka Baballoq, Suka Crmljane, the Baballoq settlement, and the Agro-Combinat behind the Baballoq settlement. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So the accounts that you were receiving from the Albanian refugees that you were interviewing included the suggestion that police were firing from the settlement itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but after 20th, because then the refugees started leaving the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And did you manage to conduct any investigation yourself about the deployment of Serb police or military in and around the Babaloc refugee camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I drove - and this sounds fantastic, but I did - I drove to Agro-Combinat. I left Albanian researchers in some of the villages near Djakovica. I drove to Agro-Combinat behind to check that. And I didn't see any movements there. But bear in mind we are talking about 29th, and I think that all of this already happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- between 20th or 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Come back to the 22nd or so in a moment or two. We have heard from a man called Rade Repic, who was the commander of a PJP company of the MUP, who arrived to relieve another PJP company in May, and he has told us that in May, the greater part of his company, 130 to 150 men, was deployed in the area of the Baballoq settlement with observation posts on Suka Baballoq and on the outskirts. Now, did you see whether there were any deployments on Suka Baballoq?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But "Suka" means actually top of the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that. But it was April. He's talking about May?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Quite correct. But you had received reports of shooting from Suka Baballoq in April, had you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Suka Babaloc and Suka Crmljanska.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. But you weren't able to check whether in fact there were MUP or PJP forces in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, actually the settlement was empty when I was there. Literally empty. Nobody except these three people sitting there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I again -- may I again ask you to make a short break between question and answer. Where you said about the reports of shooting from Suka Babaloc in April, you said Suka Babaloc and Suka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suka Crmljanska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: He's also testified that when he -- his men were deployed there, they were occupying the physical accommodation in the refugee camp closest to the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be quite possible. That's what Albanian witnesses testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's what they were telling you. And they were telling you that in April as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were telling that in April, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. So although you didn't see MUP --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- when you went to the Agro-Combinat, your -- the accounts that you were receiving were consistent with there being --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May. But can I say I had some reserves about that, because in -- in reality first time when I heard that special -- that more troops are coming and almost preparing for the conflict was beginning of May, mid of May, and I understand with a researcher who went also to Decani to the interview to interview Serbian refugees there that she was not allowed to go up to the youth hostel because there was some police forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 42, as I've understood it, in the second sentence, you say: "My information from the refugees was that the MUP were patrolling regularly the area."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, do you mean the area around the Baballoq settlement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Babaloc settlement, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And the refugees that you were referring to in that settlement, they would be Serb refugees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or Montenegrin.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Serbian or Montenegrin refugees. Did you manage to establish then exactly where those patrols were situated during April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS SST7/28 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They just complained that nobody was helping them except Serbian police that are visiting them from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. And just coming to the incidents that you describe between the 18th and 28th of April, I just wanted to see if you could help us with one matter, please. Just bear with me one second. Could we please pull up on the screen Exhibit P84. And this will need to be not shown to the public, because it has been admitted under seal, as I understand it.
